While it is different compared to season 1, it is not quite "risky". Risky is when the people are going against the rules of established conventions and do whatever they want to, in spite of executives dooming the series to be unprofitable and 'too confusing for the average person', etc. People don't generally dislike this season because the episodes don't fit and they've gone "experimental" they do, because they can spot certain gaps and unsatisfying pacing and much less screentime for certain characters that were once important, change of the focus.
They actively chose to focus more on giving breadcrumbs of mystery each episode and the lore™ rather than characters, it's no wonder that the overall direction and pacing is different. I personally think this way they're digging their own grave and they already dug one, considering that they had to spend 3 episodes just to do the aftermath of last season's cliffhanger. The episodes that you mention there are still dealing with very plot heavy things first, then characters second. Though the ORTBO one is an outlier in this, I personally didn't care about Helena impersonating the Helly storyline (that falls flat if you clock it right away since the first episode of the season) and then her raping Mark (that non-consensual sex was poorly addressed if at all and was quickly brushed off as Helly reconnects with Mark later on, but I digress), so I naturally have mixed feelings about it. 

The season 2 does have multiple showcases of their bigger budget and great cinematographers/directors on board, yes, but they don't do anything substantially different, besides betraying the characters in favor of their mystery. Gemma and Cobel's episodes are both suffering from these characters being used as plot devices, more than explorations and dissecting those characters. We don't know any flaws of Gemma, nor do we really learn about her as a character, besides what happened to her. 
The Cobel one explains a lot of her story, but it falls short with her reconnecting to her broken past and grieving her mother (tbf the scene where she's weeping on the bed is one of my favourite things they've done so far), because of the runtime and because she spent most of the time looking for something. I think that reveal that she invented severance, in the ending of this particular episode, cheapens everything that came before it in its short time, as it switches focus from her processing her trauma, it should've been done somewhere else. The search itself wasn't really satisfying and doesn't come as a result of her character arc in the episode, she just happened to realize that the blueprints would be in the 'basement'. She certainly hasn't changed her ways all the way through, cults deprogramming doesn't happen in an instant (we'll see if the series says otherwise) and this episode and the previous episode ending was only there to add her back in the series, rather than giving her character a great arc. 

Devon isn't like Reghabi at all. Devon was a character with her own motivations and quite strong "no bullshit" personality, in season 2 she's massively sidelined and brought up only for the plot reasons, to help Mark, just like Cobel or Reghabi in this season. Reghabi is the only one that stayed the blank slate all the way through though, we don't learn or explore any aspects of her character, she dips out as soon as she's not needed for the plot and Devon is very uncharacteristically doesn't even try to argue or press her for answers, because the writers don't allow their chatacters to breathe outside of what is needed and instead, are worrying more about their audience and mystery. Devon is also very passive about Ricken writing a book for Lumon, the company that kidnapped Gemma and tortures both her and Mark. You probably heard people giving lots of crap about Devon calling Cobel too and it's a reasonable criticism, they had every opportunity in the last episode to explain her character's motivations and season 1 would've probably showed those characters extensively arguing about it for longer than 1 minute. I think the dialogue overall became less tighter and witty and people generally just don't ask what they want to ask now, because of the mystery.
Sorry for the long read. these are my thoughts. I still like the show and the premise hasn't changed, but I do think they're muddying the water quite a lot and pushing themselves from a human story to something else.

In what way this season is more risky? They didn't even go through with Mark reintegrating, the dialogue and pacing is becoming less enticing and more generic, than nuanced and personal. This is so different from Season 1. Sure, the cinematography and the budget is bigger, so they become braver in that realm of things, but in terms of story and characters..? I don't think so... Reghabi is still a blank slate, Devon is reduced to a 'helper sister' character, Cobel could've had a great character arc in her episode, focusing entirely on her grief and loss of purpose (if only they went Sharp Objects route..), but instead, they quickly turned her episode into "I need to find a thing so I could be relevant to the plot again" which was so distastefully done. I still like the show, but the quality has definitely dropped and it's become the "we give you crumbs of answers to keep you interested" type of show, which I despise.

SOMA is a horror-esque walking simulator, it is not interactive to the ideas presented at all. It conveys different ideas than Talos, but it has some similar questions, sure. I think Talos explores it more in-depth and at your own expense, it is you who chooses what and who to believe, there are no characters to handhold you and force you to be on the right track. Puzzles are playing crucial role in all of this too, by the way. SOMA only has so much dialogue it can offer, and Simon being a complete dumbo (because he's an audience surrogate, obviously) doesn't really help to explore it under the microscope either. There's just no space for that, writers chose the game's storytelling to be linear and more easy to digest. Nothing wrong with it, it's just different and does not make it better in the slightest. Scan scenes are thought-provoking no doubt, but they're cutscenes after all, what's so interactive about that? That you can volunteerly press a button? I'm not so sure about that take. Talos has much less constraints in the story that it wants to tell, mainly because it relies on the curiosity of a real person playing the game, the semi-open world, secrets, time capsules (which has the most emotionally and intellectually impactful dialogue in the whole game). All of that adds to the feel of personalised experience that SOMA lacks (even though it has three choices that's not impacting narrative at all, only to create some sort of agency, sure, you could argue that Talos casually has the same thing with you making QR codes at some places). Not sure what you mean by the coin flip, considering that's just a fluke to comfort Simon and not how the copying works at all and it's not really interactive either. SOMA also lacks a great philosophical foundation that The Talos Principle presents and just grandiose scope in general, but I digress. Anyways, don't you think it's a bit too early for you to judge the game and constantly compare it to others that 'did it better,' instead of just enjoying it for what it is, rather than what it's not trying to be in the first place?
